t: #2282 Number of People That Can Be Seen in a Grid
o: Each person sees people strictly right or strictly below them such that everyone in between is shorter than both endpoints. Note equal heights block visibility (an equal-height person in between is not 'shorter'), but the target person itself may be equal height. With a 400x400 grid, an O(mn) monotonic-stack pass per row and per column is ideal; naive pairwise scanning is O(mn^2) and risky.
k: Process each row left-to-right and each column top-to-bottom with a decreasing stack of indices.
When person j arrives, everyone popped is visible (count them), plus one more if the stack is non-empty (the first taller/equal blocker).
Pop equal heights before pushing so an equal-height person correctly blocks people behind them.

a.n: Approach 1: Monotonic stack per row and column
a.i: For a fixed line of people, the ones visible from position j are exactly the strictly increasing suffix of heights looking rightward. A decreasing stack captures this: popping shorter people counts them as visible, and a remaining stack top is the first blocker, adding one more visible person. Apply independently to rows (rightward view) and columns (downward view) and accumulate.
s: For each row, scan left to right: pop strictly shorter indices adding to count; add 1 if stack non-empty; pop equal heights; push j; add count to answer.
Repeat for each column top to bottom.
a.t: O(mn) — each index is pushed and popped at most once per row and per column.

w: Verify with example 1: row [3,1,4,2,5] gives [2,1,2,1,0]. The classic pitfall is equal heights: they must block visibility of anything beyond them, hence the extra pop-equals step. A brute-force O(mn(m+n)) scan also passes at these constraints but is worth avoiding. Follow-up: visibility in all four directions, or streaming updates to heights.
